fields.value: Manuscript agreement and literary fit bear on different stages of a passage’s history. Agreement among surviving witnesses makes a late interpolation less likely, because the passage had already entered their recoverable common ancestry. Yet that agreement cannot by itself show that the common ancestor contained no earlier editorial addition. Conversely, a contextual seam can support an early-redaction hypothesis, but it does not neutralize unanimous external attestation or establish when the proposed change occurred. The rational conclusion is comparative and provisional: confidence in interpolation should rise only when a dated compositional account explains the alleged seam while also bearing the historical cost imposed by stable transmission.

Historical origin and present value come apart because they depend on different evidence and standards. If a saying was added later, it may lose force as testimony about what Jesus said while retaining philosophical, literary, or spiritual merit in what it teaches. If it is authentic, that pedigree alone does not make its teaching wise or humane. Keeping two ledgers prevents either judgment from covertly deciding the other: textual criticism can revise claims about provenance without declaring a passage worthless, and admiration cannot convert canonical acceptance into historical proof. The distinction therefore preserves critical openness while explaining how doubt about authorship can coexist with serious appreciation of the Bible.
